summary: Presents use cases from diverse industries that need deterministic flows, meaning guaranteed bandwidth, bounded latency, and similar properties for time-sensitive data. They differ in topology and behavior and give context for Deterministic Networking (DetNet). It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 8578 describes industries that need predictable network timing and reliability. It records their use cases and common requirements to inform Deterministic Networking design.

subtitle: Industry use cases for deterministic network flows

tldr.problem: Industries including utilities, manufacturing, cellular radio, and professional media need traffic with bounded latency, guaranteed bandwidth, or very low loss.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes use cases, current approaches, future needs, and requests to the IETF across nine industry areas, then summarizes common themes.
tldr.outcome: It provides context and a yardstick for DetNet design decisions. It does not specify an architecture or protocol.

facts.label: Teleprotection transfer time
facts.value: 4-8 ms for the most critical messages on 60 Hz lines

facts.label: LTE fronthaul one-way delay example
facts.value: 250 microseconds; one cited specification allows 100 microseconds

today: RFC 8578 is an Informational use-case document and the batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It provides context for DetNet design and does not define an architecture or protocol.

sections.title: Purpose of the Use Cases
sections.content:
The memo describes deterministic flows: flows with guaranteed bandwidth, bounded latency, and other properties for time-sensitive data. The use cases cover professional audio and video, electrical utilities, building automation, industrial wireless, cellular radio, industrial machine-to-machine communications, mining, private blockchain, and network slicing.

The document does not propose a specific DetNet design or protocol. It gives context for design decisions and a way to assess whether proposed designs serve the listed use cases. DetNet itself does not address clock distribution or time synchronization.
sections.plainLanguage: Different industries need network traffic to meet timing and reliability goals. This document records those needs without choosing a protocol or design.

sections.title: Professional Audio and Video
sections.content:
Professional audio and video systems are moving from point-to-point links toward packet networks. Existing deterministic flows can operate inside some Layer 2 networks, but the RFC says these flows cannot be routed over IP to connect wider areas using a standards-based Layer 3 interface.

Live playback cannot depend on retries when a packet arrives too late. Audio and video may need bounded and consistent latency to remain synchronized; the RFC gives about 33 ms as a common audio/video synchronization tolerance and notes tighter limits for sound reinforcement and phase-sensitive audio. It also describes redundant paths and sharing reserved but unused bandwidth with best-effort traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: Live audio and video cannot simply wait for a late packet to be resent. Their network paths need predictable delay and may need redundant routes.

sections.title: Utilities, Buildings, Wireless, and Cellular
sections.content:
Electrical utilities use teleprotection messages to isolate faults and protect equipment. Some messages need transfer times of 4-8 ms for 60 Hz lines. Building automation, wireless industrial networks, and cellular fronthaul also have timing, reliability, and security needs; the LTE fronthaul example gives a one-way delay budget of 250 microseconds, while a cited specification allows 100 microseconds.

These environments often use proprietary networks, dedicated links, or over-provisioned packet networks. The use cases ask for standards-based networks that can carry deterministic and ordinary traffic together, while supporting resource reservations, accurate timing, and resilience.
sections.plainLanguage: Power protection, building controls, industrial wireless, and cellular radio each have different timing limits. They seek shared networks that can meet those limits alongside other traffic.

sections.title: Industrial M2M, Mining, Blockchain, and Slicing
sections.content:
Industrial machine-to-machine systems exchange periodic control data, and mines use networks to monitor or remotely control vehicles and equipment. Private blockchain systems may benefit from lower network latency during consensus. Network slicing divides shared infrastructure into logical networks and may use DetNet for resource isolation or deterministic service within a slice.

The RFC notes limits: DetNet is point-to-point or point-to-multipoint, while some slicing use cases need multipoint-to-multipoint guarantees. Its scalability also limits the number of flows it can carry, though flow aggregation and queue-management changes may help.
sections.plainLanguage: Factories, mines, blockchain systems, and network slices have additional needs for predictable delivery. The RFC also notes that DetNet may not fit every multipoint use case.

sections.title: Common Themes Across the Use Cases
sections.content:
The common themes include open, standards-based networks; central administration; integration of Layer 2 and Layer 3; and coexistence of deterministic and best-effort traffic. Packets in a DetNet flow are intended not to be dropped because of congestion, although this is not a guarantee against media or checksum errors.

Unused reserved bandwidth can be made available to best-effort traffic, but not to other time-sensitive traffic without its own reservation. The use cases call for bounded latency and jitter, high availability, redundant paths, and isolation between reserved flows. The RFC states that DetNet scope excludes unbounded decentralized networks such as the Internet.
sections.plainLanguage: The use cases share a need for isolated flows, predictable delay, and backup paths. Unused reserved capacity can serve best-effort traffic until its reservation is needed.
